claims.text: The starting material is a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without secondary phases or additives.
Graphene nanoplatelets can be dispersed within the CoCrFeNi matrix during alloy synthesis.
A small volume fraction of graphene nanoplatelets will form a stable, adherent lubricious film during high-temperature sliding.
The graphene-derived film will maintain low friction from room temperature to 800 °C.
The graphene-derived film will maintain low wear rates from room temperature to 800 °C.
Dispersed graphene reacts with an oxidizing environment under elevated-temperature mechanical stress to form a protective tribofilm on the worn surface.
Graphene nanoplatelets provide solid lubrication at lower temperatures.
As temperature rises, slight oxidation of graphene produces a stable carbonaceous tribolayer.
The tribolayer mitigates wear by decreasing direct metal-to-metal contact.
The tribolayer mitigates wear by redistributing contact stresses.
The graphene-modified alloy will have a significantly lower coefficient of friction than unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout the test regime.
The graphene-modified alloy will have a significantly lower wear rate than unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout the test regime.
The graphene-modified alloy will retain particularly notable tribological performance at temperatures approaching 800 °C.
The proposed effect applies under dry or low-humidity sliding conditions.
The proposed effect is limited to loads and speeds that do not cause matrix melting or excessive oxidative degradation.

contradictions.description: The conditions permit an inert atmosphere, but the proposed elevated-temperature mediator specifically requires reaction with an oxidizing environment and the mechanism relies on oxidation of graphene. No alternative high-temperature film-formation pathway is given for inert testing.
